doc.title: Shelly Berg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Technology, demos and competition in composing
summary: Berg considers the pitfalls of synthesized demos and loops, which create the atmosphere of great music without composing talent, and the greater competition; the piano itself still reveals new things.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Do you think the tools that are available today — how should I say this — don’t foster that kind of ability?

It’s a concern. It’s great in that you can immediately hear in terms of trial and error and learning to hear and getting to hear back what you’ve written. It’s a great tool, with the caveat that you’re not really hearing back what you’ve written. And chances are it may sound a whole lot better or a whole lot worse in a real environment. So there’s certainly some use to it. I find in the industry now everybody wants a full demo of any orchestra piece you write. And you can get it to sound so good that they think it’s what it’s going to sound like and yet it isn’t and there’s a really worry there. Because they might not quite get it from the demo and yet it sounds convincing enough that they think they’re hearing the real thing. So it’s fraught with those pitfalls. But yeah, I think that — you know there was an interesting column, I think it was in Jazz Times a couple of years ago. And what it said I agree with, and basically it said that technology makes it possible for everyone to create the atmosphere of great music. You can put on your Will Lee bass loop and your Peter Erskine drum loop and lock up the BPM and you’ve got that, and then you’ve got the greatest sampled sounds and this and that and the other, and you can basically put something together that the sounds sonically are first rate. That doesn’t even begin to speak to what you are as a composer or what aptitude you have for that. But you’ve now created the atmosphere that you’re doing it. And I guess the same could be said in graphics, with computer graphics and all those kinds of things. There is difference between artists who can really draw something and somebody who can just merge a bunch of stuff off of a computer program. So in some ways an interesting dichotomy has happened. With the explosion of media kinds of outlets, there is much more opportunity as a composer, but there is also much, much more competition from people who twenty
years ago could never have been in this business. And it becomes hard to separate them out.
That’s true. If you go and you search CD Now and everyone has a web site, which you can say is a good thing because everyone has the opportunity. But how do you find out who belongs there?
I suppose in a sense the people who were in it before this technological explosion can tend to feel a little threatened unless they keep up with it.
And it’s difficult to keep up with it. If you buy the right magazines what it tells you every week is that you’re behind now. Buy this.
So but every time I sit down at a piano, it’s a technology that hasn’t changed in a long time.
And it’s still revealing new things to me every day.
